The two tones as they are realized in isolation are- high tone (H) marked by ‘´’ and low tone (L) marked by ‘`’ as shown in (15).

tone_statements.quote: Being a Tibeto-Burman language, Chiru also has the tonal system. There are two tones in Chiru, viz. (a) falling tone /*/ and (b) level tone /~/. Falling tone is marked and level tone is not marked.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement about stress: every opened source (Awan 2017 thesis, Singh 2007 thesis, plus the previously read Grierson 1904 and Awan 2014/2017/2019 articles) is silent on word stress/accent. The only divergence is in the description of the tone system: Awan 2017 analyses two register tones (high vs low, Praat-based) while Singh 2007 labels the two tones level vs falling; both agree Chiru has exactly two contrastive tones.

tone.says: Chiru is tonal with a register system of two tones, High (acute) and Low (grave), contrastive on monosyllables (minimal pairs án 'curry' / àn 'to lean back', méi 'fire' / mèi 'to sleep', tár 'old' / tàr 'clumsy', lú 'difficult' / lù 'head'), analysed in Praat with spectrogram figures 8-10; every syllable carries an underlying tone; no distributional restrictions with onsets, vowels or codas (Table 16).
